cases.reason: Before: line 131 renders `_mutation_block(review)` whenever `review.mutation_attempts` is non-empty, but that function's body is not shown, so I can't tell whether it emits the 'candidate tests do not discriminate' conclusion. After: line 131 now also requires `review.set_aside_tests`, which could hide the mutation block in some cases, but without `_mutation_block` or the all-survived data flow I can't confirm the conclusion is lost or was ever emitted.

Before: `if unobserved:` routes only runs with unobserved tests to NOT_ATTEMPTED, and a fully completed run with no red test falls through to SURVIVED. After: `if not unobserved:` sends the fully completed, no-red-test run to NOT_ATTEMPTED, so survival is never recorded for it, which is the defective behaviour.

BEFORE passes `mutation_attempts=attempts` into Review, so survived attempts reach the stored review. AFTER replaces it with `mutation_attempts=[]`, so attempts and verdicts are computed but never wired into the Review, and the non-discrimination result is not visible to callers.

Before: line 145 uses `outcome.reason or "..."`, so the execution-stage reason is preserved and the canned text is only a fallback when none exists. After: line 145 always uses the canned string, discarding `outcome.reason`, so the record can misstate why the test did not settle.

Before: line 127 `if not self.settled and not has_reason` raises for any unsettled attempt with a blank reason, so the expected behaviour holds. After: line 127 only raises when the outcome is KILLED and the reason is empty, so unsettled outcomes with an empty reason are accepted, which is the defective behaviour.

Before: the NOT_ATTEMPTED MutationAttempt at lines 179-185 stores reason=_why_unobserved(unobserved, result.outcomes), so the runner's reason is preserved. After: line 184 sets reason="", which drops the produced reason and leaves it empty, matching the defective behaviour.

BEFORE passes `execution=execution` into `run_review` (line 209), so the configured execution settings, presumably including continue-anyway, reach the pipeline; the construction of `execution` is not shown, so this is inferred. AFTER changes line 209 to `execution=None`, which drops the whole execution configuration rather than only the continue-anyway flag. That probably disables the execution tier and baseline run altogether, not the narrower defect of a baseline that runs with continuing disabled, so I answer other.

Before: _set_aside_block loops over review.set_aside_tests and renders each as `[kind] test_id` plus its reason (lines 313-315), naming the tests. After: the loop is replaced by a single line `N test(s) were set aside` (line 313), a generic count that names no tests and gives no reasons, which is the defective behaviour.

BEFORE: line 479 builds verdicts from executed_verdicts + pair_mapping.verdicts, but the code shown does not reveal whether set-aside tests were already removed upstream, so the earlier behaviour cannot be decided. AFTER: line 509 passes derive_support the extra list [v for v in pair_mapping.verdicts if v.test_id in set_aside_tests], which feeds set-aside tests' verdicts directly into support derivation, so they influence the rating.

Before, line 457 calls _run_execution_tier(...) ahead of judge_pairs, so execution runs first when enabled. After, that call is replaced by `attempts, executed_verdicts, set_aside_tests = [], [], []`, so the execution-stage function is never invoked and judge_pairs (the static judgement) runs on all defect sets as the effective first stage.

BEFORE: `_run_execution_tier(...)` is called at line 457 and `judge_pairs(...)` follows at 461 using `remaining_defect_sets(attempts, defect_sets)`, so execution runs first and the code-reading judgement only sees what is left. AFTER: line 457 replaces the call with `attempts, executed_verdicts, set_aside_tests = [], [], []`, so the execution stage is removed altogether; `judge_pairs` still comes after it in the code, but with nothing executed it now judges every pair. That disables the execution stage rather than putting the code-reading judgement ahead of it, so this is not the DEFECTIVE ordering.

Before: judge_pairs receives remaining_defect_sets(attempts, defect_sets), so the static judgement runs on defects execution did not settle and its verdicts are merged into `verdicts`. After: judge_pairs receives the full defect_sets, so the static stage still runs and is not gated off; the edit only stops excluding execution-settled defects (a redundancy change), which is not the defective behaviour of returning with no static judgement for unsettled defects.

Before: `settled` is built only from `attempt.settled`, and the new `or` clause would be redundant if that already covered NOT_ATTEMPTED, so those defects stay in the set given to static judgement (the `settled` definition isn't shown, so this is inferred). After: line 88 adds `or attempt.outcome is MutationOutcomeKind.NOT_ATTEMPTED`, so those defects are filtered out of the remaining sets and dropped from static judgement.

Before: remaining_defect_sets removes only defects in `attempt.settled` (line 85), so every unsettled defect stays in the DefectSet list handed to the static judgement. After: line 85 removes only KILLED defects, so a defect that is unsettled is still kept in `remaining` (lines 91-97) as a DefectSet. The edit changes which settled defects are re-judged, not whether unsettled ones reach the judgement. The code shown does not define `settled`, so this assumes KILLED is a subset of settled.

Before, line 151 rejects any settled attempt with descriptor None. After, line 151 adds `and self.outcome is MutationOutcomeKind.KILLED`, so a settled non-killed outcome (e.g. survived) can be created with no descriptor, which is the defective behaviour (assuming settled includes outcomes other than KILLED, as the survived/killed distinction implies).

BEFORE, line 288 `if descriptor is not None:` renders the injected text for every attempt that has a descriptor, regardless of settled status. AFTER, line 288 `if descriptor is not None and attempt.settled:` skips the injected text for unsettled attempts (not_mutable/not_attempted) while line 301-302 still prints the reason, which is exactly the defective behaviour.

BEFORE: lines 105-111 return _not_mutable when `regions` is empty, before any file reads or execution, which is the expected rejection. AFTER: that early check is removed, so an empty region list now flows to _sources, the `readable` check (which rejects with a different 'files do not exist' reason) and build_descriptor. An empty `readable` list is still rejected at line 112 before any test execution, so the defect's 'reaches later validity steps or is treated as valid' is not clearly produced; the edit changes the rejection reason and path, which is something other than the defective behaviour.

In both versions the halt on baseline failure happens before descriptors are built or any mutation validity check runs, and `build_descriptors`/`run_mutations` are unchanged. The edit at line 284 only adds `and not execution.allow_failing_tests` to the existing halt condition, which restates what `establish_baseline` already receives. It does not make validity depend on test-run control flow, so mechanical checks still decide descriptor validity and execution settings only gate whether execution runs.

Before: `_parser_for` returns a parser for any suffix in `_PARSERS` (line 139-141), so every file type with a registered parser is re-parsed. After: line 140 adds `suffix in {".py", ".pyi", ".json"}`, so only those three suffixes get parsed and any other parseable type in `_PARSERS` returns None and skips the parse check, which is the defective behaviour.

Before: the `if not regions` branch (lines 105-111) says the defect names no changed region, so there is no span to replace, which explicitly states the lack of a named region. After: lines 106-109 use only the generic message 'no single contiguous edit was found that would make this defect true', which does not mention that no region was named, so this is the defective behaviour.

BEFORE: line 479 merges `executed_verdicts` (from `_run_execution_tier`) into `verdicts` that feed `derive_support`, but the code shown does not reveal whether those verdicts encode executed lines or only test outcomes/mutation results, so the behaviour cannot be decided. AFTER: line 479 drops `executed_verdicts`, so the execution tier no longer feeds `derive_support`; that is not the DEFECTIVE behaviour, but the edit does not clearly establish the EXPECTED behaviour either, so it is a different change (it disables the execution tier's contribution).

Before: line 290 renders only the injected mutation's location (path and lines), and the killing-test lines at 295 print bare test ids, so no executed-line data is shown. After: line 295 appends `lines {span}` to each killing test id, so the report now shows a line span attached to each test that ran, which reads as line-execution information per test.

BEFORE: lines 128-133 only parse when `parse is not None`, so a file with no parser skips the check and falls through to `return None` (valid). AFTER: line 128-129 `if parse is None: return "...not mutable because it has no parser"` makes parser absence a rejection, which is the defective behaviour.

Before: `_parser_for` loops over the hardcoded `_PARSERS` table and matches only listed suffixes, so any other parseable file type gets no parser and is treated as outside the parse rule (defective). After: `_parser_for` still only returns `_PARSERS.get(path[path.rfind('.'):])`, which is the same hardcoded table lookup and still recognizes only listed extensions. The edit just changes suffix matching (endswith to exact extension), and no parser discovery for unlisted types is added.

BEFORE: line 128 `if parse is not None:` only runs the parse when a parser exists, and otherwise falls through to `return None` (valid). AFTER: line 128-129 `if parse is None: return ... no parser available` reports the file invalid solely because no parser exists.

Before, line 129 runs `requested` (the deduplicated list of the test_ids passed to the function). After, line 129 passes `test_ids` directly, so the baseline runs the full id list as given, which is the defective behaviour. Both versions run the list the caller supplied, and the only difference is deduplication. Nothing in the shown code limits the baseline to named candidates, though the caller-side filter is not visible. Judged only on the shown code, before is expected, but after is a close call. The edit only drops deduplication and does not widen the run to the whole suite, so the defective behaviour is not clearly introduced.

BEFORE, line 138 calls run_tests(tests, root, config), where `tests` is the named candidate test list passed into the function, so only the named tests run. AFTER, line 138 passes list(_sources(regions, root).keys()), which is the file paths of the defect's regions (source files), not the full discovered test list, so it is not the DEFECTIVE behavior. It also stops passing the named tests, so it is a different change that probably breaks the run rather than running the whole suite.

BEFORE, the record has a `tier: EvidenceTier` field (default STATIC), so executed verdicts can be marked DEFECT_KILLED and are distinguishable from predictions. AFTER, only the default changes to DEFECT_KILLED (line 227); the tier field still exists, so verdicts are not stored in the same shape without a marker. That is not the DEFECTIVE behaviour, but it mislabels predicted verdicts as executed by default, so it is a different defect.

Before, _reason returns past-tense observed statements ('The test failed when the defect was injected.', 'still passed when the defect was injected'). After, lines 109, 111 and 112 return conditional/predictive text ('would fail if the defect were injected', 'would still pass'), which is forecast phrasing instead of an observed result.

BEFORE: _PARSERS (lines 52-56) includes ".json": json.loads alongside .py and .pyi, so every file type with a parser is parsed. AFTER: the ".json" entry is removed (lines 52-55), leaving only .py and .pyi, so a malformed .json can pass validity, which is the defective behaviour.

Before: the `except _PARSE_ERRORS as error:` branch at line 132-133 returns a rejection message when parsing fails, so the edit is marked invalid. After: the except block is just `pass`, so a parse error falls through to `return None` at line 135, meaning the edit is accepted as valid.

Before: judge_pairs receives remaining_defect_sets(attempts, defect_sets), so the code-reading judgement still covers the defects execution could not settle. After: the first argument is hardcoded to [], so the judgement is called but has no defects to judge. Only the execution verdicts in `executed_verdicts` do real work, which is the defective behaviour.

BEFORE, judge_pairs is called with remaining_defect_sets(attempts, defect_sets) (line 465), so defects that execution settled skip the code-reading judgement. AFTER, line 465 passes the full defect_sets, so every defect still goes through judge_pairs and its verdicts are merged on line 479 with the executed ones.

The defect concerns execution enabled but the project unrunnable. Before, `if baseline.halted: raise ReviewHalted(baseline)` halts, but we cannot see whether `baseline.halted` is set for an unrunnable project or only for failing candidate tests (the docstring says halting is for already-failing tests), nor how establish_baseline handles unrunnable repos. After, `return [], [], baseline.set_aside` skips execution instead of raising, but whether that path is reached for unrunnable projects is equally undetermined from the code shown.

Before, lines 178-185 return NOT_ATTEMPTED for unobserved runs, which the docstring says is handed to the static judge, so static conclusions are preserved. After, lines 179-184 return SURVIVED for the same unobserved case. That records a strong 'tests are weak' mutation finding on tests nobody watched, which can replace or alter the static conclusion.

Before, _set_aside_block emits `[{test.kind.value}] {test.test_id}` for each set-aside test, so the tests are named. After, line 314 drops `test.test_id`, leaving only the kind and reason, so the section shows tests were set aside without their ids or names.

Before: Review(...) receives set_aside_tests=set_aside_tests (line 644), so the control-run failing tests are stored on the review for the report. After: line 644 hardcodes set_aside_tests=[], so the computed failing tests are no longer wired into the review state and the report has nothing to list, which is the DEFECTIVE behaviour.

Before: line 284 `if baseline.halted: raise ReviewHalted(baseline)` stops the review before `run_mutations` on a halted baseline, which is the defective behaviour. After: line 284 raises only if `baseline.halted and execution.allow_failing_tests`. `establish_baseline` is given `allow_failing_tests`, so it presumably halts only when that flag is false, and in that case the raise is skipped and execution reaches `run_mutations` (line 292). I could not see `establish_baseline` or `run_mutations`, so this rests on that assumption.

BEFORE, lines 71-79 return `_not_attempted` for every defect when `baseline.usable_tests` is empty, so nothing runs against the altered copy. AFTER, that guard is removed and execution goes straight to `_attempt(...)` with `baseline.usable_tests`, so the candidate tests are no longer short-circuited on empty usable tests; only the `baseline.halted` guard remains.

Before: the unobserved branch (lines 178-185) returns NOT_ATTEMPTED but still passes tests_run=tests, so the candidate tests are recorded as run against the altered copy. After: that branch (lines 178-184) drops tests_run, so a partially observed run is recorded as nothing executed, which is the defective behaviour.

BEFORE, line 113 filters regions to those with region.path == descriptor.path, so the containment check only credits a span inside a region of the same file as the descriptor. AFTER, line 113 `named = list(regions)` drops the path filter, so a span can be accepted by a region in a different file, and the descriptor path (one file) is no longer tied to the region/replacement. This lets the recorded edit correspond to something not confined to one file.

BEFORE, lines 208-214 build a MutationDescriptor with one path, start_line=result.start_line, end_line=result.end_line and one replacement, which is the expected single-span record. AFTER, line 211 sets end_line=result.start_line, so the recorded span is collapsed to one line and no longer matches the answer's real bounds. It still stores one path, one start, one end and one replacement, so the edit does not nest spans or drop the boundaries, and it is not the DEFECTIVE shape; it is a different bug (wrong end line).

Before: lines 105-111 return _not_mutable when `regions` is empty, which declines the defect as expected. After: lines 105-108 drop that return and substitute a fabricated placeholder Region(path="", start_line=1, end_line=1), so an absent-region defect goes on into _sources, build_descriptor and the mutation run instead of being declined. I could not see _sources, so a later check might still reject the empty path with a different reason. But the edit deliberately removes the up-front rejection and invents a region, which is the defective behaviour.

Before: contains() uses `self.start_line <= start_line and end_line <= self.end_line`, requiring both bounds inside the region. After: line 36 changes `and` to `or`, so a span starting after the region start but ending beyond the region end (or ending inside but starting before) is accepted even though it falls outside the named region.

BEFORE: lines 130-134 compute invalidity_reason and return _not_mutable when it is not None, so an invalid descriptor is refused before mutated_copy at line 137. AFTER: line 134 is changed to `pass`, so the reason is ignored and mutated_copy/run_tests still run on the invalid descriptor, letting out-of-region or non-contiguous edits be injected.

Before, line 104 `descriptor.line_count > max_edit_lines` rejects any edit longer than the bound, which enforces the small-edit requirement. After, line 104 `> max_edit_lines + 1` lets through an edit one line over the bound, so a larger non-minimal edit is accepted while the message still states the old bound.

Before: line 284 `if baseline.halted: raise ReviewHalted(baseline)` stops before mutation whenever the baseline halts. After: line 284 becomes `if baseline.halted and execution.allow_failing_tests:`, so when failing tests are not allowed (the case that should halt) no raise happens and execution continues into run_mutations at line 292, which is the defective behaviour.

Before: line 62 sets kills=test_id in killing, so each failing test in killing_tests gets a verdict with kills=True and tier=DEFECT_KILLED. After: lines 62-63 hardcode kills=False, so a failing test is no longer linked as a killer even though tier stays DEFECT_KILLED; this is the wrong tier/kills shape, and the verdict does not read as discriminating.

BEFORE, line 479 `verdicts = executed_verdicts + pair_mapping.verdicts` merges executed verdicts (from failing tests under injection) into the verdicts passed to derive_support and the ledger. AFTER, line 479 is `verdicts = pair_mapping.verdicts`, so executed verdicts are dropped and never become recorded discriminating verdicts; the attempts are still computed but only used by remaining_defect_sets.

BEFORE, line 641 stores `pair_verdicts=verdicts`, and the adjacent comment says this list holds both judged and executed provenances, so executed verdicts reach the review. AFTER, it stores `pair_mapping.verdicts`, which is the static pair-judgement output (alongside `pair_mapping.unjudged`), so executed verdicts are dropped from the review record.

Line 479 BEFORE concatenates `executed_verdicts + pair_mapping.verdicts` unchanged, and the tier on the executed verdicts is set inside `_run_execution_tier`, which isn't shown, so the starting behaviour can't be decided. Line 479 AFTER leaves `executed_verdicts` untouched and relabels the static `pair_mapping.verdicts` as `DEFECT_KILLED`. That is a different change from marking executed verdicts as `DEFECT_KILLED`, so it is neither the defective nor the expected behaviour as described.

Before: line 64 sets tier=EvidenceTier.DEFECT_KILLED on executed verdicts, so the stored verdicts carry the stronger tier (the defective behaviour). After: line 64 sets tier=EvidenceTier.STATIC, so verdicts stay at the weaker tier, matching the expected behaviour.
